content: Turmeric, scientifically known as Curcuma longa, is a rhizomatous herbaceous perennial plant that belongs to the ginger family, Zingiberaceae. It is native to tropical regions of South Asia. The plant thrives in temperatures ranging from 20°C to 30°C and requires substantial annual rainfall for optimal growth. The rhizomes of the plant are harvested annually, and a portion of these rhizomes is replanted for the next growing season. Turmeric is sometimes misspelled or mispronounced as tumeric and is referred to as kunyit in certain Asian countries. The rhizomes of turmeric are boiled for several hours, dried in hot ovens, and then ground into a deep orange-yellow powder. This powder is widely used as a spice in South Asian cuisines, particularly in curries, as well as for dyeing and imparting color to mustard condiments. The active ingredient in turmeric is curcumin, which gives it an earthy, bitter, and peppery flavor, along with a mustard-like aroma. The town of Sangli, located in the southern part of Maharashtra, India, is recognized as the largest and most significant trading hub for turmeric in Asia, and possibly the world. Uses Food Turmeric is extensively used in various food products, including canned beverages, baked goods, dairy products, ice cream, yogurt, yellow cakes, biscuits, popcorn, sweets, cake icings, cereals, sauces, and gelatins. It is a key ingredient in most commercial curry powders. When used as a food additive, turmeric is coded as E100 and is employed to protect food products from sunlight. The oleoresin extracted from turmeric is used in oil-based products, while curcumin solutions or powders dissolved in alcohol are used in water-based products. Over-coloring with turmeric is sometimes applied to compensate for fading in products like pickles, relishes, and mustard. In combination with annatto (E160b), turmeric is used to color cheeses, yogurt, dry mixes, salad dressings, winter butter, and margarine. It is also used to impart a yellow hue to prepared mustards, canned chicken broths, and other foods, often as a cost-effective substitute for saffron. Turmeric is a staple spice in Indian and South Asian cooking and is used to flavor traditional dishes such as Nepali meat dumplings (momos). Medicine In Ayurvedic medicine, turmeric is believed to possess numerous medicinal properties. It is commonly used in India as an accessible antiseptic for cuts and burns. For minor injuries, turmeric powder is often applied as a home remedy. Ayurvedic practitioners also claim that turmeric contains fluoride, which is thought to be beneficial for dental health. Additionally, turmeric is used as an antibacterial agent and is consumed as a dietary supplement in some Asian countries to address stomach issues and other ailments. In Okinawa, Japan, turmeric tea is particularly popular. Turmeric is currently being studied for its potential therapeutic benefits in conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease, cancer, and liver disorders. It has also gained attention as a treatment for depression under the name Ava. Western scientists have increasingly recognized the medicinal properties of turmeric in recent years. According to a 2005 article in the Wall Street Journal titled Common Indian Spice Stirs Hope, research into curcumin, the active compound in turmeric, has surged. The U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) is conducting clinical trials to investigate curcumin's efficacy in treating pancreatic cancer, multiple myeloma, Alzheimer’s disease, and colorectal cancer. A 2004 study at UCLA-Veterans Affairs suggested that curcumin might inhibit the accumulation of destructive beta-amyloid plaques in the brains of Alzheimer’s patients and could potentially break down existing plaques. Gregory Cole, a professor of medicine and neurology at UCLA, noted that curcumin has been used for thousands of years as a safe anti-inflammatory agent in traditional Indian medicine. Another 2004 study at Yale University demonstrated that oral administration of curcumin to mice with cystic fibrosis restored physiologically relevant levels of protein function. Curcumin has also shown anti-tumoral effects against melanoma cells. A North Carolina-based pharmaceutical company, Curry Pharmaceuticals, is studying the use of curcumin cream for psoriasis treatment, while another company markets a curcumin-based cream called Psoria-Gold, which has shown anecdotal promise in managing the disease. Recent research involving mice has indicated that turmeric may slow the spread of breast cancer to the lungs and other parts of the body. It also enhances the effectiveness of the chemotherapy drug taxol in reducing breast cancer metastasis. Curcumin is believed to be a potent pain-relieving agent (antinociceptive). A study published in the November 2006 issue of Arthritis & Rheumatism demonstrated turmeric's effectiveness in reducing joint inflammation and recommended clinical trials to explore its potential as a treatment for alleviating arthritis symptoms. Turmeric is thought to act as a natural inhibitor of the COX-2 enzyme and has shown efficacy in animal models of neuropathic pain secondary to diabetes, among other conditions. Cosmetics Turmeric is used in the formulation of certain sunscreens. In India, some women apply turmeric paste to reduce unwanted hair growth. It is also a traditional practice in parts of India and Pakistan to apply turmeric paste to brides and grooms before marriage, as it is believed to enhance skin glow and protect against harmful bacteria. When mixed with milk and applied to the skin, turmeric acts as an excellent anti-scarring agent. The Thai government is funding a project to extract and isolate tetrahydrocurcuminoids (THCs) from turmeric. These colorless compounds, distinct from tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), are believed to have antioxidant and skin-lightening properties and may be useful in treating skin inflammations, making them valuable for cosmetic formulations. Dye Turmeric is not an ideal fabric dye due to its poor lightfastness, meaning it fades easily when exposed to light. Gardening Turmeric can be used as a natural ant repellent. Although the exact mechanism by which turmeric deters ants is unknown, anecdotal evidence suggests its effectiveness. Chemistry Turmeric contains up to 5% essential oils and up to 3% curcumin, a polyphenol. Its chemical name is (1E,6E)-1,7-bis(4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl)-1,6-heptadiene-3,5-dione. Curcumin can exist in at least two tautomeric forms: keto and enol. The keto form is more stable in the solid phase, while the enol form is preferred in solution.
